- If sentiment is positive (≥0.2) in recent history, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast by 1–3% for next period.
- If sentiment is negative (≤0.0), model often underestimates; increase forecast by 1–3% to account for downward surprise.
- After a sharp price spike (e.g., >10% from prior period), model frequently overcorrects; cap forecast increase to 2–5% for next period.
- If true outcome shows mean reversion (e.g., price drops after peak), model often fails to adjust; reduce forecast slope by 10–20% in subsequent periods.
- For 30-day forecasts, model consistently overestimates in early periods (e.g., 2023-02) — apply downward bias of 2–5% for first 5–7 days.
- If sentiment history shows repeated 0.00 values, model tends to be flat; introduce slight upward drift (0.5–1.5%) if price is trending up.
- In low-sentiment periods with high volatility, model underestimates downside risk — add 1–2% buffer for negative deviation.
- If true outcome shows strong divergence from history (e.g., >15% from 18-day mean), model often fails to capture it — adjust forecast to align with recent 3–5 day average.
